title: Descending int[]
prompt: `int[] nums = {3, 1, 2};` then `Arrays.sort(nums, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(b, a));` — what happens?
options: Compile error — there is no `Arrays.sort(int[], Comparator)`; comparators only sort object arrays
nums becomes `{1, 2, 3}` — the comparator is ignored
It compiles but throws at runtime
explanation: Comparators compare objects, and `int` is a primitive, so no such overload exists. Sort ascending and reverse, or copy into an `Integer[]` and sort that with `Collections.reverseOrder()`. `int[][]` is fine: each row is an `int[]` object.

title: Which way does it sort?
prompt: `Arrays.sort(pairs, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(b[1], a[1]));` sorts the pairs…
explanation: `Integer.compare(b[1], a[1])` — b before a — reverses the order; index [1] picks the second element.

title: Sort by start, tie on end
prompt: Sort intervals ascending by start; equal starts break ties by smaller end first.
explanation: Primary key in (a, b) order = ascending. Only when the starts are equal does the second `Integer.compare` on the ends decide. This exact sort opens Merge Intervals.

title: Recall: Comparator builders
explanation: `comparingInt(keyFn)` sorts ascending by an int key, `.reversed()` flips everything built so far, and `.thenComparingInt(keyFn)` adds a tie-breaker. The explicit `(int[] r)` type is needed because Java can't infer a lambda's parameter type once you chain onto it.

title: Sort by length, then alphabet
prompt: Return `words` sorted by length ascending; equal lengths alphabetically. Sort the input array with a comparator and return it.

solution.explanation: Object arrays (String[]) accept comparators directly in Arrays.sort. The comparator checks length first and only calls `compareTo` (alphabetical) on a tie. Equivalent builder form: `Comparator.comparingInt(String::length).thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder())`. O(n log n) comparisons.

hints: Two keys: length is the primary one, the word itself only breaks ties.
Compare lengths with `Integer.compare`; if they're equal, fall back to `a.compareTo(b)`.

title: Drill: sort intervals by start
prompt: From memory: sort the `int[][] intervals` in place ascending by start value and return it — the one-liner that begins every intervals problem.

solution.explanation: Each row is an `int[]` object, so `Arrays.sort` takes a comparator that compares the rows' start values. `Integer.compare` stays correct at the int extremes where `a[0] - b[0]` overflows. O(n log n).

hints: `Arrays.sort` on an `int[][]` accepts a comparator that receives two rows.
Compare the start of each row: index `[0]`, with `Integer.compare(a[0], b[0])`.

title: Descending ints via Integer[]
prompt: Return a new `int[]` containing `nums` sorted in **descending** order. `Arrays.sort(int[])` can't take a comparator, so box the values into an `Integer[]`, sort that with `Collections.reverseOrder()`, and copy back.

solution.explanation: Boxing to `Integer[]` makes the array sortable with a comparator; `Collections.reverseOrder()` flips the natural order without any subtraction, so the extremes are safe. Copying back unboxes. O(n log n). (Sorting ascending and reversing in place also works and avoids boxing.)

hints: Comparators need objects. Which wrapper array can hold the same values?
Copy `boxed` back into a fresh `int[]` — assignment unboxes each element.

title: Comparable vs Comparator
prompt: What's the key difference between implementing `Comparable` and passing a `Comparator`?
options: Comparable defines a class's own natural order (compareTo); a Comparator is an external ordering supplied at the sort call
They're the same thing with different names
Comparable is for numbers, Comparator is for Strings
explanation: Comparable bakes one default ordering into the class (`compareTo`); Comparator lets you specify any ordering externally, including several different ones for the same type.

title: Recall: implement Comparable
prompt: Complete the class declaration and the compareTo method (order Persons by age).
explanation: `implements Comparable<Person>` plus a `compareTo(Person)` returning a negative/zero/positive int gives the class a natural order.

title: Recall: comparator forms
prompt: Fill in the ascending and descending comparator lambdas.
code:
Arrays.sort(arr, (a, b) -> Integer.{{1}}(a, b));       // ascending
Arrays.sort(arr, (a, b) -> Integer.compare({{2}}, {{3}})); // descending
explanation: `Integer.compare(a, b)` sorts ascending; swap the arguments to `(b, a)` for descending. Prefer this over `a - b`, which can overflow. (Here `arr` must be an object array such as `Integer[]`.)

title: Drill: sort rows by first element (desc)
prompt: From memory: sort `pairs` (each an `int[]`) by their first element in DESCENDING order, in place, and return it.

solution.explanation: Passing `b[0]` before `a[0]` reverses the natural order, so larger first elements come first. The sort is stable, so rows with equal first elements keep their input order. O(n log n).

hints: Ascending would be `Integer.compare(a[0], b[0])`. What reverses it?
Swap the arguments: `(a, b) -> Integer.compare(b[0], a[0])`.
